sourceCopy.name: Histogram Calculator
sourceCopy.title: Histogram Calculator Free | UsefulVerse
sourceCopy.description: Make a histogram from your data. Choose bin rules, compare counts or density, and download a chart or frequency table for free.
sourceCopy.intro: Paste up to 5,000 numbers to build an equal-width histogram. Choose an automatic bin rule or set the bin count, then view and export the frequencies.
sourceCopy.howQuestion: How do I make a histogram?
sourceCopy.howAnswer: Enter numeric data and choose a bin rule. The calculator divides the data range into equal-width intervals, counts each value once, and includes the maximum value in the final interval.
sourceCopy.privacyAnswer: No. The histogram is calculated in this browser. Your values are not uploaded or saved by this tool.

fields.dataHint: Separate values with spaces, semicolons or new lines. Semicolons keep decimal commas intact.
fields.accuracyNote: Supports 1–5,000 finite values with absolute magnitude at most 10⁹ and 1–50 equal-width bins. The last interval includes its right endpoint. Relative frequency and density are normalized to all entered values. If Freedman–Diaconis cannot use a positive IQR/range, it falls back to Sturges. This is a descriptive chart, not a statistical inference or probability model.
fields.freedmanFallbackNote: The interquartile range or data range is zero, so the Sturges rule was used instead.
fields.equalValuesNote: All values are equal; the display range was expanded so the chart remains visible.

messages.checkInputs: Check the data and histogram settings.
messages.copyUnavailable: Copy is not available in this browser.

additionalFaqs.question: Which bin rule should I use?
additionalFaqs.answer: Sturges is a simple starting point for smaller samples. Square-root uses the square root of the sample size. Freedman–Diaconis uses the interquartile range and can adapt to spread and outliers. You can also choose the bin count yourself.

additionalFaqs.question: What is the difference between frequency and density?
additionalFaqs.answer: Frequency counts values in each interval. Relative frequency shows the percentage. Probability density divides relative frequency by interval width, so the total bar area is one.

additionalFaqs.question: Does the final bin include its upper bound?
additionalFaqs.answer: Yes. Bins are half-open intervals except the final bin, which includes the maximum data value so no value is left out.
